subtopic_detail: Post-UTI imaging cascade after typical first UTI
stem:
A 14-month-old girl completed a 3 day course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a first febrile urinary tract infection two weeks ago. Urine culture from a clean catch specimen grew Escherichia coli at greater than 10 to the 8 CFU per litre, sensitive to the antibiotic used. Fever settled within 36 hours and she has been well since.

Antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal and postnatal renal function has never been checked. She had a normal newborn examination and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. She is up to date with immunisations, growing along the 50th centile for weight and length, and toilet training is not yet established. There have been no further urinary symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with no palpable masses, external genitalia normal, back and spine unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that imaging is not required and give safety-netting advice for future febrile illnesses
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine renal tract ultrasound after a single typical E coli UTI in a child aged over 6 months who responded within 48 hours of antibiotics, has normal antenatal imaging, and no atypical features. Safety-netting for early reassessment of any future febrile illness is the appropriate outpatient plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks with paediatric review of the imaging result
options.rationale: Routine post-UTI ultrasound is a NICE construct, not the RCH pathway. RCH reserves ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrence, non-E coli organism, sepsis, or infants under 6 months without antenatal imaging - none apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning at 4 to 6 months post-illness to assess for cortical scarring
options.rationale: DMSA is a NICE-recommended follow-up but does not appear in the RCH cascade. The RCH pathway does not use DMSA for a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux as an underlying cause
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive, involves urinary catheterisation and ionising radiation, and is not part of the RCH post-UTI cascade for a single typical UTI. It is reserved for selected children with recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Commence low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg nocte for 12 months with paediatric clinic review
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a single typical E coli UTI in a low-risk child. Trials such as PRIVENT show modest benefit only in selected higher-risk populations, and prophylaxis is not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: This child had an uncomplicated typical E coli UTI that responded promptly to first-line antibiotics. The RCH cascade for imaging after paediatric UTI is more restrictive than NICE and does not require routine imaging in this setting. Safety-netting for early urine testing during any future febrile illness is the correct plan.
key_points: RCH indications for post-UTI ultrasound: age under 6 months without antenatal imaging, atypical UTI, non-E coli organism, poor response at 48 hours, or recurrent UTI
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and are not in the RCH cascade
Antibiotic prophylaxis has a narrow AU indication and is not first-line for a single typical UTI
explanation.pearls: The single strongest driver of over-investigation of paediatric UTI is applying NICE algorithms in Australia. Anchor to RCH and its atypical-UTI trigger list.

stem:
A 5-year-old boy weighing 22 kg attends a general practice for review after his second episode of anaphylaxis to cashew nut, this time triggered by an accidental exposure at kindergarten. On the first exposure two months ago he developed urticaria, lip swelling and audible wheeze that resolved with intramuscular adrenaline administered by paramedics.

Skin prick testing performed by an allergist has confirmed cashew and pistachio sensitisation with wheal sizes above the diagnostic cut-off. He has no other atopic disease, takes no regular medication, and there is no personal or family history of arrhythmia. Both parents have completed ASCIA anaphylaxis first aid training and are able to demonstrate correct injector technique on a trainer device.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: unremarkable

lead_in: Which adrenaline autoinjector prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
options.rationale: The 150 microgram device is reserved for children weighing 10 to 20 kg. At 22 kg this child has crossed into the 300 microgram band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: Two adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
options.rationale: ASCIA prescribes the 300 microgram device for children weighing 20 kg or more using a banded weight rule. Two devices are the standard AU prescription to allow a repeat dose if symptoms do not respond after 5 minutes. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A single adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and referral to community pharmacy for a second on request
options.rationale: ASCIA advises prescribing two devices simultaneously so a second dose is immediately available at the same location if response is inadequate at 5 minutes. Waiting for a second prescription is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A prescription for oral cetirizine 10 mg daily during pollen season with an adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector as required
options.rationale: Regular antihistamine has no preventive role in food anaphylaxis and does not reduce risk. It also risks masking early urticarial signs of a reaction. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A prescription for daily inhaled fluticasone 100 microgram twice daily and two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors
options.rationale: There is no indication for inhaled corticosteroid without a diagnosis of asthma, and 150 microgram is the wrong band for a 22 kg child. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded weight rule for paediatric adrenaline autoinjectors: 150 microgram for 10 to 20 kg and 300 microgram for 20 kg and above. Two devices should be prescribed together so a repeat dose is available at 5 minutes if needed. This 22 kg boy requires two 300 microgram devices.
key_points: ASCIA banded doses: EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 10 to 20 kg, EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg and above
Prescribe two devices simultaneously; the repeat dose is given after 5 minutes if response is inadequate
Oral antihistamines and daily inhaled corticosteroids have no role in preventing anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: Do not perform mg/kg arithmetic at the bedside for autoinjectors - use the ASCIA weight bands. The threshold of 20 kg is the one to remember.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

subtopic_detail: Gastroenteritis rehydration pathway after failed oral trial
stem:
A 20-month-old girl weighing 12 kg is brought to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of watery diarrhoea and vomiting after a family gastroenteritis outbreak. In the department she has been given a single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg and offered oral rehydration solution 5 mL every 5 minutes over the past 60 minutes, but has vomited three times and refuses further sips.

On examination she is fractious but consolable. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill at the sternum is 3 seconds, and skin turgor is mildly reduced. She has passed a small volume of concentrated urine 4 hours ago. Weight from a well child check 3 weeks ago was 12.5 kg. There is no bilious vomiting, no blood in the stool and no abdominal distension.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous gas pH 7.34 with bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-28)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula and commence 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 20 mL/kg over 20 minutes as a resuscitation bolus
options.rationale: A fluid bolus at this rate is reserved for shock, not moderate dehydration. Her perfusion parameters do not meet shock criteria and IV rehydration is second-line to NG in AU paeds practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Administer a second oral ondansetron 4 mg dose and continue small-volume oral rehydration solution attempts
options.rationale: The RCH single ondansetron dose for a child of this weight is 2 mg (8 to 15 kg band). A repeat dose is not recommended and 4 mg exceeds the correct band. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and commence continuous rehydration with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg/hour for the next 4 hours
options.rationale: In children with mild to moderate dehydration and failure of the oral trial, the RCH pathway is nasogastric rehydration before intravenous fluids. Continuous NG rehydration at approximately 25 mL/kg/hour over 4 hours corrects the deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Admit for observation on maintenance intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent dextrose at 44 mL per hour
options.rationale: Maintenance-only IV fluids do not correct the estimated 4 percent deficit efficiently and skip the preferred NG rehydration step. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Discharge home with instructions to continue small volume oral rehydration solution and represent if there is no improvement in 12 hours
options.rationale: Discharge after a failed oral trial with ongoing signs of moderate dehydration is inappropriate. Formal rehydration in the department is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: This 20-month-old has clinically moderate dehydration and has failed a supervised oral rehydration trial after ondansetron. The RCH pathway then favours nasogastric rehydration before escalating to intravenous therapy, which is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.
key_points: NG rehydration is first-line after failed oral trial in mild to moderate dehydration
Ondansetron single dose 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg (0.15 mg/kg banded)
IV fluids reserved for shock or failure of NG rehydration
explanation.pearls: The commonest ED anti-pattern is skipping NG rehydration and going straight to IV. The NG route corrects the deficit efficiently and avoids cannulation.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with 24 hours of fever, lethargy, and a non-blanching purpuric rash on the shins and buttocks that appeared this morning. He is now drowsy and difficult to rouse, cool peripherally to the mid-forearm, and has a prolonged capillary refill of 5 seconds at the sternum. He weighs 18 kg.

He is up to date with the National Immunisation Program schedule including meningococcal ACWY and B, and has no known allergies. His mother reports he was well enough to attend day care yesterday morning. He has no significant past medical history and is not on regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 168, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.8 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: After immediate airway assessment and application of monitoring, what is the correct order of the next four interventions?

options.text: Infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 minutes, obtain intravenous access afterwards, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
options.rationale: A fluid bolus cannot be delivered without access, and cultures should be taken before or with the first antibiotic dose whenever access is available - not after. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid. Starting adrenaline before the first fluid bolus is not the AU sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Draw a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock and impaired consciousness. It is deferred until the child is haemodynamically stable and neurologically improved. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Obtain intravenous or intraosseous access, draw blood cultures, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences access first, then cultures, then first-hour antibiotics, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes. Antibiotics must not wait for cultures if cultures cannot be drawn promptly, but with prompt access both can be taken in sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, draw blood cultures, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is considered adjunctively in pneumococcal meningitis and is given with or before the first antibiotic dose, but it should not replace timely antibiotic delivery in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

explanation.summary: This child has septic shock with purpuric rash suggestive of meningococcaemia. The RCH pathway requires immediate access, cultures, and first-hour antibiotics, followed by 20 mL/kg saline boluses titrated up to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes come only after fluid-refractoriness. LP is deferred while shock persists.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, first antibiotic, 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Antibiotics within 1 hour is the AU standard - do not delay for cultures if access is difficult
Adrenaline / noradrenaline reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg crystalloid
explanation.pearls: Meningococcal purpura with shock is a national safety pathway. Cef 100 mg/kg IV up to 2 g is the AU empiric dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

stem:
A term female neonate born at 38 plus 4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery is reviewed on day 4 of life in the postnatal ward. Her mother is blood group O rhesus positive and the baby is A rhesus positive with a direct antiglobulin test negative and blood groups matched. She is exclusively breastfed with a 6 percent weight loss from birth and is otherwise well.

A transcutaneous bilirubin at 24 hours was 90 micromol/L. On clinical examination today at 96 hours of age she looks jaundiced to the mid-abdomen with normal tone, a strong cry, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Serum total bilirubin drawn is 320 micromol/L, predominantly unconjugated. Full blood count is unremarkable and reticulocyte count is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: total bilirubin 320 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 8 micromol/L, DAT negative, haemoglobin 175 g/L (150-220), reticulocyte count within normal limits, group and hold A rhesus positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an immediate double volume exchange transfusion after commencing intensive triple overhead phototherapy
options.rationale: The exchange transfusion line at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis is above 450 micromol/L. Her level is well below this. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Withhold breastfeeding for 48 hours, commence formula supplementation, and repeat the serum bilirubin level in 24 hours
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding is not recommended in AU practice and can compromise establishment. Phototherapy alongside supported breastfeeding is preferred. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Reassure the family that this represents physiological jaundice and arrange community midwife home review in 48 hours
options.rationale: The bilirubin level at 96 hours has crossed the phototherapy threshold and cannot be observed with community review only. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Send urgent haemolysis screen including G6PD, pyruvate kinase and haemoglobin electrophoresis before starting treatment
options.rationale: With DAT negative, blood groups matched, and normal reticulocyte count and haemoglobin, urgent haemolysis screen is not the priority. Phototherapy should not wait for further tests. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Commence single overhead phototherapy, repeat the serum bilirubin in 6 hours, and continue breastfeeding with lactation support
options.rationale: At 96 hours of age a term infant with no haemolysis crosses the AU-adapted NICE phototherapy line at approximately 310 to 320 micromol/L, warranting single phototherapy and a repeat level to check response. Breastfeeding continues alongside. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: At 96 hours of age a term neonate with an unconjugated bilirubin of 320 micromol/L and no haemolysis has crossed the phototherapy line on the AU-adapted NICE chart. Treatment is single phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and a 6 hour repeat level. Exchange transfusion is a separate, much higher line reserved for severe or resistant hyperbilirubinaemia.
key_points: Phototherapy threshold at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis approximates 310 to 320 micromol/L
Exchange transfusion line is much higher (about 450 micromol/L) and unmet here
Continue breastfeeding with support; do not interrupt for phototherapy alone
explanation.pearls: Read the phototherapy chart by age in hours, not days. The line rises sharply over the first 96 hours and plateaus after that.

sources.label: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is reviewed in a paediatric assessment unit on day 6 of daily high fevers that have not responded to alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen. His parents describe non-purulent bilateral conjunctival redness that started on day 3, a strawberry appearance to his tongue since yesterday, and a rash on his trunk that has come and gone.

He has no cough, coryza, or diarrhoea. Blood tests today show a C-reactive protein of 90 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/hour, platelet count of 480 x10 to the 9 per litre, and mild sterile pyuria on urinalysis. Liver enzymes show an alanine aminotransferase of 90 U/L (less than 40). A recent throat swab for group A streptococcus is negative and there are no oral vesicles or exudate. There is no lymphadenopathy over 1.5 cm and no peripheral desquamation yet.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: CRP 90 mg/L (less than 5), ESR 60 mm/hour, platelets 480 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), ALT 90 U/L (less than 40), albumin 30 g/L (35-50), urinalysis with sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an urgent echocardiogram and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Fever for 5 or more days with 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, elevated ALT, low albumin) meets the AHA incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. Treatment with IVIG plus aspirin should not wait for the echocardiogram. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Continue supportive care with paracetamol and reassess in 48 hours before considering any specific therapy
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 doubles the risk of coronary aneurysm. Fever on day 6 with matching criteria warrants treatment now. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin for suspected scarlet fever and repeat throat swab in 48 hours
options.rationale: Group A streptococcal throat swab is negative and there are no oral or pharyngeal features to support scarlet fever. Antibiotic therapy will not address the underlying vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as first-line monotherapy pending confirmation of coronary artery involvement
options.rationale: Steroids are used as adjuncts to IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-refractory disease, not as first-line monotherapy in AU practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Arrange a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg for suspected meningitis
options.rationale: There are no meningitic features and the presentation over 6 days with mucocutaneous features points to Kawasaki disease, not meningitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Prolonged fever with fewer than 4 principal Kawasaki criteria but supportive laboratory features fulfils the incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. IVIG plus aspirin should be started promptly. Delay beyond day 10 markedly increases the risk of coronary artery aneurysm.
key_points: Incomplete KD: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 principal criteria, plus supportive labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, raised ALT, low albumin)
IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
Do not delay treatment for echocardiogram - the two can proceed in parallel
explanation.pearls: The single strongest predictor of long-term coronary sequelae is IVIG delay past day 10. Recognise the incomplete pattern early.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

stem:
A 12-day-old term boy is brought to a rural emergency department at 3 a.m. by his parents who noticed poor feeding for the previous 24 hours and cool, mottled legs this morning. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, discharged at 24 hours after a normal newborn examination and passed the pre-discharge pulse oximetry screen with post-ductal saturation of 96 percent. He is exclusively breastfed and had been feeding well until yesterday.

On examination he is pale, grunting, and lethargic. The upper limbs are warm and pink; the lower limbs are cool and dusky. Right upper limb blood pressure is 88/48; right lower limb blood pressure is 40/22. There is a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a hyperdynamic praecordium. Femoral pulses are just palpable and delayed compared with the brachial pulses. Liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 176, blood pressure 88/48 right arm and 40/22 right leg, respiratory rate 68 with grunting, SpO2 pre-ductal 98 percent and post-ductal 90 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 5.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), chest x-ray with cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion, four-limb blood pressures with a 40 mmHg upper to lower limb gradient
data_table.Post-transfer arrangements: the nearest paediatric intensive care retrieval team has been contacted and estimated time of arrival is 90 minutes

lead_in: In addition to initial resuscitation, what is the single most important pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer an intravenous adenosine 100 microgram/kg rapid bolus for suspected supraventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: Sinus tachycardia at 176 with a differential four-limb blood pressure and a chest x-ray consistent with heart failure is not SVT. Adenosine will not correct ductal closure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 nanograms/kg/minute after securing peripheral access
options.rationale: A late-presenting ductal-dependent left-sided lesion such as coarctation or interrupted aortic arch reopens with prostaglandin E1. The infusion is started before intubation or catheter placement in a shocked newborn to restore lower body perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

options.text: Commence an intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/minute as first-line vasoactive support
options.rationale: Inotropes increase myocardial oxygen demand in an unrelieved obstruction. Prostaglandin reopening of the duct treats the underlying cause and is the correct first pharmacological step. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

options.text: Administer an intravenous frusemide 1 mg/kg bolus with fluid restriction for pulmonary venous congestion
options.rationale: Diuresis will worsen an already-hypotensive systemic circulation and does nothing for the closed duct. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

options.text: Administer an intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg dose for empirical late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reasonable adjuncts but do not address the underlying ductal-dependent lesion. Prostaglandin is the single most important pharmacological intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)

explanation.summary: The pre and post ductal saturation differential, four-limb blood pressure gradient, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis in a 12-day-old point to a critical left-sided ductal-dependent lesion whose duct is closing. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and restores lower body perfusion; it should be started before any other pharmacological intervention while awaiting retrieval. Passing the pulse oximetry screen does not exclude the diagnosis because the post-ductal saturation is initially maintained by the patent duct.
key_points: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 ng/kg/min reopens the arterial duct in ductal-dependent lesions
Four-limb blood pressures showing an upper to lower gradient over 20 mmHg suggest coarctation or interrupted arch
The pulse oximetry newborn screen picks up right-sided but not all left-sided lesions - late collapse is possible
explanation.pearls: Any collapsed neonate presenting in the second week should have prostaglandin E1 started empirically while echocardiography is arranged. Apnoea is the main dose-related side effect - be prepared to intubate.

sources.label: Australian Newborn Pulse Oximetry Screening Statement

stem:
A 4-month-old former term infant presents to a tertiary paediatric ED in July with three days of coryza, worsening cough and feeding half his usual volume. He is alert but has moderate subcostal recessions and audible wheeze. Nasal swab PCR is positive for RSV.

His mother reports his lips looked slightly grey on the drive in, though they now look pink. He has never had wheeze before, was born at 39 weeks, and had no neonatal respiratory support.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 87% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly dehydrated, wet nappy 4 hours ago; widespread fine crackles with expiratory wheeze; no focal consolidation
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, pCO2 45 mmHg, HCO3 23 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: High-flow nasal cannulae at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92%
options.rationale: HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after 2 hours per RCH; jumping straight to HFNC bypasses the guideline step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Facemask oxygen at 6 L/min with SpO2 target 94 to 98 percent
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis target is SpO2 90 percent, not 94 to 98; facemask flow is also excessive first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Low-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH CPG makes low-flow nasal cannula the first-line oxygen delivery in bronchiolitis with SpO2 90 percent as the target; HFNC only after 2 hours of low-flow failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with supplemental oxygen delivered via mask
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months as beta-2 receptor density is insufficient for benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised 3 percent hypertonic saline with room air observation off oxygen
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not routinely used in Australian bronchiolitis pathways, and off-oxygen management with SpO2 87 percent is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in Australian tertiary practice follows the RCH CPG oxygen escalation ladder. Low-flow nasal cannula oxygen is first-line for hypoxia, with SpO2 90 percent as the accepted floor. HFNC is stepped up only after two hours of low-flow failure, and bronchodilators are not indicated under 12 months. Aggressive early HFNC does not reduce ICU admission and delays escalation to appropriate senior review.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent, not 92 to 94.
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen is first-line; HFNC after 2 hours of failure.
Salbutamol is not recommended under 12 months.
NGT feeds are preferred over IV in mild to moderate dehydration.
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis pathway targets SpO2 90 percent on low-flow nasal cannula 1 to 2 L/min before considering HFNC after 2 hours; do not chase 94 to 98 percent saturations.

stem:
A 20-month-old girl is brought to a regional ED at 2 am with a 24-hour history of coryza and a barking cough that started that evening. On arrival she has audible inspiratory stridor when upset but none at rest, and mild suprasternal tug when crying.

She settles quickly on her mother's lap and takes sips of juice. She has had no fever, no drooling and no cyanotic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful when settled, barking cough on stimulation; chest clear apart from transmitted upper airway sounds; oropharynx normal
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed; clinical Westley score 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose?

options.text: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily for three days as a course
options.rationale: Prednisolone has been shown less effective than single-dose dexamethasone for croup and is not the AU first-line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally as a single dose observed in ED
options.rationale: RCH CPG uses dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally as a single dose then discharge
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the severe-croup dose per RCH; a Westley score of 2 is mild and does not require it. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once with observation for two hours
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is a fallback if oral dexamethasone is refused or vomited; oral is preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with 3 hours observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest, not mild presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: The RCH croup pathway separates mild and severe management by dexamethasone dose. Mild and moderate croup receive 0.15 mg/kg orally as a single dose; severe croup receives 0.6 mg/kg orally with nebulised adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline requires a minimum three-hour observation window because of rebound stridor risk after the effect wears off. Prednisolone is not recommended as an alternative because relapse rates are higher.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally, single dose.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally plus nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 is a flat dose (not per kg).
Minimum three-hour observation after last adrenaline dose.
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is the RCH default for mild to moderate croup; escalate to 0.6 mg/kg only when stridor is present at rest with recessions.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl weighing 12 kg presents with two days of profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. On arrival she has dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor and a capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Her mother has been offering water and diluted juice but she has vomited all attempts in the last three hours.

Her weight two weeks ago at a GP visit was 12.7 kg. She has been alert throughout the assessment and stopped vomiting after receiving oral ondansetron thirty minutes ago in triage. Blood glucose on finger prick is 4.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, dry lips, delayed skin turgor, sunken eyes; abdomen soft, no guarding; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally
data_table.Investigations: Weight loss 5.5 percent from baseline; blood glucose 4.1 mmol/L; urea and electrolytes not yet available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration approach now?

options.text: Continue small volume oral rehydration solution sips over the next four hours
options.rationale: Oral trial has already failed with vomiting; further oral-only attempts risk under-resuscitation despite the ondansetron effect. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes then reassess
options.rationale: IV boluses are reserved for shock or severe dehydration; central capillary refill 3 seconds with preserved BP and alertness is moderate, not severe. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent glucose infusion over 24 hours
options.rationale: Slow IV replacement bypasses the NGT step that RCH mandates when oral rehydration fails and dehydration is mild to moderate. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Nasogastric rapid rehydration with oral rehydration solution over four hours
options.rationale: For mild to moderate dehydration where oral has failed, RCH makes nasogastric rapid rehydration first-line over IV; equally effective and avoids cannulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Admit for observation and re-attempt oral rehydration solution in six hours
options.rationale: Delaying active rehydration with ongoing losses risks progression to severe dehydration and worsening electrolyte disturbance. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: RCH gastroenteritis pathway places nasogastric rapid rehydration ahead of intravenous fluids when oral rehydration has failed in a child with mild to moderate dehydration. NGT rehydration matches IV for rate of correction with fewer complications and no cannulation. IV bolus is reserved for shock or severe dehydration (weight loss more than 9 percent, altered conscious level, poor peripheral perfusion). Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg once (2 mg for 8 to 15 kg) improves oral tolerance and reduces IV need.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration failing oral.
IV bolus is reserved for shock or severe dehydration.
Ondansetron 2 mg (8 to 15 kg) supports oral tolerance.
Weight loss is the most reliable dehydration marker.
explanation.pearls: For a 12 kg toddler with 5 to 6 percent weight loss and failed oral trial, NGT ORS at 25 mL/kg/hour for four hours is RCH first-line; do not skip to IV.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy weighing 15 kg presents to a GP clinic after eating a cashew biscuit at daycare. Ten minutes later he developed generalised urticaria, then hoarse voice and now audible stridor.

His mother had brought his previously prescribed EpiPen Jr for daycare use but has not administered it. He has been alert throughout but is becoming agitated. He is a known cashew-sensitised child with previous mild reactions but no prior anaphylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but agitated; generalised urticaria; audible stridor; increased work of breathing; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: No time for investigations; call for ambulance already made

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms via EpiPen Jr into anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded IM adrenaline: 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr) for 10 to 20 kg body weight; this child is 15 kg. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms via EpiPen into anterolateral thigh
options.rationale: 300 microgram EpiPen is the ASCIA band for 20 kg and above; overdose in a 15 kg child risks tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg diluted and titrated to response
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis with cardiac monitoring after two IM doses have failed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow facemask oxygen
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically only and does not reverse systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 75 micrograms drawn from ampoule based on weight
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded dosing not mg/kg arithmetic to reduce dose errors; 75 micrograms is under-dosed and is not a recognised band. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded IM adrenaline table rather than mg/kg calculation to reduce dose errors under stress. The 10 to 20 kg band receives 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr), and 20 kg and above receives 300 micrograms (EpiPen). IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses fail and requires cardiac monitoring. Nebulised adrenaline is a symptomatic adjunct for airway oedema only.
key_points: 10 to 20 kg: EpiPen Jr 150 micrograms IM.
20 kg and above: EpiPen 300 micrograms IM.
Banded dosing beats mg/kg arithmetic under stress.
IV adrenaline reserved for refractory cases with monitoring.
explanation.pearls: ASCIA banded adrenaline: 150 mcg for 10 to 20 kg, 300 mcg for 20 kg and above; the mg/kg calculation is a distraction that causes dose errors.

stem:
A 5-week-old male infant is brought to ED by his parents with a two-hour history of poor feeding and one axillary temperature of 38.4 degrees C at home. He is a former term infant of an uneventful pregnancy and was well until this evening.

On arrival he is alert, moves symmetrically and takes 20 mL of formula in front of you. His anterior fontanelle is flat, no rash is present and his mother reports he is different from his usual self.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 48/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C rectally
data_table.Examination: Alert, moves symmetrically, tone appropriate; no rash; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; chest and abdomen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine dip: leucocytes negative, nitrites negative; CRP 12 mg/L (less than 5); WCC 14.5 x10^9/L; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management step?

options.text: Observe overnight with hourly paediatric early warning scores and repeat inflammatory markers in six hours
options.rationale: RCH mandates full septic workup and empirical IV antibiotics for any fever in an infant under 3 months, not observation alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin at 30 mg/kg discharge home with paediatric review at 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and discharge are unsafe for an infant under 3 months with a documented fever regardless of appearance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Perform blood culture only then start empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for observation
options.rationale: Blood culture without lumbar puncture in an infant under 3 months misses meningitis, which changes duration and choice of antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Chest x-ray then empirical oral cefalexin with paediatric outpatient review at 24 hours
options.rationale: Imaging first without a full septic screen and IV antibiotics is not the RCH pathway for infants under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Full septic workup with lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: RCH requires full septic screen (blood culture, urine catheter or SPA, CSF) and empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin for any infant under 3 months with fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: Any infant under 3 months with a documented fever mandates a full septic workup because clinical assessment is unreliable and meningitis can present without focal signs. RCH requires blood culture, catheter or SPA urine, and lumbar puncture before empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin for GBS and Listeria cover. Reassuring appearance and normal CRP do not remove the LP requirement. Wait until CSF is obtained before giving the first dose only if it will not delay antibiotics beyond one hour.
key_points: Any fever in infant under 3 months triggers full septic workup.
LP is included unless clinically contraindicated.
Empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin covers Listeria and GBS.
Do not delay antibiotics beyond one hour for procedures.
explanation.pearls: Fever in an infant under 3 months means blood, urine and CSF cultures then IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin within 60 minutes; do not observe.

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid rate and cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 7-year-old girl weighing 22 kg presents with a two-day history of polyuria and polydipsia and today, vomiting and drowsiness. She has newly diagnosed diabetes based on a random glucose of 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.1 mmol/L, and venous pH 7.10.

Her initial GCS was 14 (E3 V5 M6) on arrival and she has received a single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes. Sodium is 132 mmol/L and corrected sodium is 141 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is 6 mmol/L. She has just been re-examined 30 minutes after the bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min (Kussmaul), SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils equal 3 mm reactive, mildly complaining of headache; abdomen soft, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 27 mmol/L, ketones 6.1 mmol/L, pH 7.11, HCO3 6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (corrected 141), potassium 4.9 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give another 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes and continue rehydration
options.rationale: Further boluses in a child with a falling GCS and worsening headache during DKA rehydration risk precipitating overt cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; APEG DKA guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes and reduce fluid rate to maintenance
options.rationale: Deteriorating GCS with headache mid-rehydration is presumptive cerebral oedema; RCH and APEG recommend immediate mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes and fluid rate reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately to reverse ongoing ketosis
options.rationale: Insulin without addressing the cerebral event and while GCS is falling does not treat the emergent problem; APEG delays insulin one hour after fluid start regardless. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is associated with cerebral oedema and is not indicated at pH 7.11; it is reserved for pH under 6.9 with cardiovascular compromise. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Change intravenous fluid to 0.45 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent glucose over the next hour
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluids in early DKA rehydration accelerate cerebral oedema risk; RCH keeps isotonic fluids until glucose falls below 15 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA and typically emerges 4 to 12 hours into rehydration. Warning signs include falling GCS, new headache, bradycardia, hypertension, and pupillary changes. The APEG and RCH DKA pathways specify immediate mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes (or hypertonic saline 3 percent 2.5 to 5 mL/kg) and a reduction in fluid rate on presumptive cerebral oedema. Isotonic fluids and delayed insulin (one hour after fluid start) are used across the whole rehydration phase to minimise osmolar shift.
key_points: Falling GCS plus headache mid-rehydration is cerebral oedema until proven otherwise.
Mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 15 minutes is first-line.
Isotonic fluids only until glucose below 15 mmol/L.
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA unless pH under 6.9 with shock.
explanation.pearls: Neurological deterioration during paediatric DKA rehydration is cerebral oedema; mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV within minutes and halve the fluid rate.

sources.label: APEG DKA in children and adolescents 2020

stem:
A 14-month-old girl presented four days ago with fever, foul-smelling urine and a positive catheter urine culture growing more than 10^8 CFU/L of Escherichia coli fully sensitive to trimethoprim. She was commenced on oral trimethoprim and has been afebrile within 36 hours.

Antenatal ultrasounds at 20 and 32 weeks gestation were normal. She has been feeding normally, growing along her expected centile, and has had no prior urinary tract infections. Her mother asks what imaging her daughter now needs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well hydrated, playful; abdomen soft with no palpable masses; genitalia normal appearing
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim; creatinine 32 micromol/L (within paediatric range); resolution of fever within 36 hours of therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan now?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during this illness within 48 hours of admission
options.rationale: RCH restricts illness-phase renal ultrasound to atypical UTI: poor response to 48 h antibiotics, non E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, or raised creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) at completion of antibiotic course
options.rationale: MCUG is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH pathway for a single typical UTI; do not order routinely. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No imaging indicated; safety net advice for recurrent urinary symptoms only
options.rationale: RCH does not require imaging after a single typical UTI even under 24 months when antenatal scans were normal; safety net for recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA renal cortical scan at four to six months to assess renal scarring
options.rationale: DMSA is not part of the RCH cascade for a single typical UTI; it is a NICE tool, not AU standard practice here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound routinely at four to six weeks post infection
options.rationale: Routine post-infection ultrasound is not required for a single typical UTI under 24 months per RCH when antenatal monitoring was normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: RCH deliberately narrowed UTI imaging following evidence that most abnormalities were antenatally detected. A single typical UTI in a well child under 24 months, responding to antibiotics with normal antenatal scans, needs no imaging. Illness-phase ultrasound is reserved for atypical features (poor response, non-E coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine). DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and not routine in the RCH pathway.
key_points: Typical UTI plus normal antenatal scans equals no imaging.
Illness-phase ultrasound only for atypical UTI features.
DMSA and MCUG are not routine in RCH.
Follow-up ultrasound only for recurrent UTI or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Under RCH, a typical E coli UTI in a well child under 24 months with normal antenatal scans needs no imaging; do not default to DMSA or MCUG.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy has had a fever above 39 degrees for 6 days despite 48 hours of oral amoxicillin. His parents report cracked red lips, red eyes without pus, and a fine truncal rash that comes and goes. On examination he is irritable but not toxic, with a single 20 mm right anterior cervical node. Palms and soles are not swollen or peeling. Throat swab for group A streptococcus and blood culture are negative.

He has no household exposure to measles, no travel history and is fully immunised. The ED registrar has already arranged a formal echocardiogram, which shows a left anterior descending coronary artery Z score of +2.7.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cracked lips, bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection, polymorphous truncal rash, single 20 mm right anterior cervical node; hands and feet not swollen; no BCG scar reaction
data_table.Investigations: CRP 142 mg/L (<5), ESR 74 mm/hr, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 78 U/L (<40), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sterile pyuria 40 leucocytes/HPF; blood culture and throat swab negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IVIG 2 g/kg intravenously over 10 hours together with high dose aspirin
options.rationale: Fever over 5 days plus 3 principal features and supportive labs (CRP over 30, platelets over 450, sterile pyuria, ALT elevation, albumin under 30) plus a coronary Z score over +2.5 meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria and mandates IVIG within 10 days of fever onset per the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Await the fifth principal clinical feature before starting definitive therapy
options.rationale: The AHA and RCH algorithms explicitly treat incomplete disease that meets supplementary lab criteria plus coronary changes; delay increases aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as sole first-line anti-inflammatory therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first-line in Australia; steroids are used with IVIG in high risk groups (Kobayashi score high, under 12 months, coronary dilation at diagnosis), not alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Escalate to intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed occult bacterial infection
options.rationale: Blood culture is negative, and the syndrome is not compatible with occult sepsis; antibiotics do not treat the underlying vasculitis and delay definitive care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge with 48-hour ambulatory review and antipyretic advice at home
options.rationale: Coronary dilation is already present and the risk of progression to aneurysm is highest within the first 10 days; discharge would miss the treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is common in preschool children and easily missed because fewer than 4 principal features are present. AHA and RCH algorithms treat when fever exceeds 5 days plus 2 or 3 principal features and supportive labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30, elevated ALT, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria) OR any coronary Z score over +2.5. IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus aspirin is standard first-line, and the treatment window is within the first 10 days of fever to minimise aneurysm risk.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on lab criteria plus coronary imaging.
IVIG 2 g/kg is the definitive treatment; aspirin is adjunct.
Coronary Z score over +2.5 alone meets treatment criteria.
Steroids are added, not substituted, in high risk cases.
explanation.pearls: In fever over 5 days with cracked lips, non-purulent conjunctivitis and a raised CRP, do not wait for the fifth criterion; check LAD Z score and give IVIG 2 g/kg if any coronary dilation is present.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement 2017: Diagnosis and Treatment of Kawasaki Disease

stem:
A term female infant born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks is reviewed on the postnatal ward at 28 hours of age because she looks yellow to the midwife. Her mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the baby's cord blood group is A positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. Birthweight was 3.4 kg, she is breastfeeding on demand and has passed meconium and urine.

She is alert, feeding well, has moist mucous membranes and normal tone. There is no cephalohaematoma and no significant bruising.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, jaundice to the chest, no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae; feeding effectively at breast
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 260 micromol/L (unconjugated); haemoglobin 165 g/L (140-220); reticulocytes 6 percent (2-6); blood film unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase breastfeeding frequency and reassess bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours
options.rationale: A bilirubin of 260 micromol/L at 28 hours in an ABO incompatible DAT-positive infant is well above the phototherapy line; observation alone risks kernicterus. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start intensive phototherapy now and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours
options.rationale: At 28 hours in a haemolytic infant the treatment line sits close to 240 micromol/L; intensive phototherapy is indicated and response reassessed within 6 hours per the RCH nomogram. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange immediate double volume exchange transfusion in the neonatal unit
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion in a stable term infant requires bilirubin to cross the exchange line despite phototherapy or the bilirubin/albumin ratio to exceed threshold; not yet indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin one gram per kilogram now
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for isoimmune haemolysis when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy or approaches the exchange line; not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Formula supplementation only with recheck of bilirubin the following morning
options.rationale: Feed supplementation without phototherapy does not adequately lower bilirubin in haemolytic disease and delays effective treatment; overnight recheck is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: The Australian bilirubin nomogram plots serum bilirubin against postnatal age in hours and adjusts thresholds for risk factors including DAT-positive isoimmune haemolysis. A DAT-positive infant with ABO incompatibility at 28 hours postnatal is high risk; phototherapy is initiated well below the standard line. IVIG and exchange transfusion escalate only if bilirubin continues to rise on maximal phototherapy or approaches the exchange line. Reassessment at 6 hours confirms response.
key_points: DAT-positive haemolysis lowers the phototherapy threshold.
Age-in-hours nomogram is the standard, not fixed bilirubin cutoffs.
IVIG is second-line if bilirubin keeps rising on intensive phototherapy.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of maximum medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: A DAT-positive ABO baby with bilirubin over 250 micromol/L in the first 24 to 48 hours crosses the intensive phototherapy line on the RCH nomogram; start phototherapy immediately and recheck within 6 hours.

stem:
A previously well 5-month-old boy is admitted with a first febrile urinary tract infection. Suprapubic aspirate grew pure Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin. He responded within 24 hours to intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and is now afebrile, feeding well and passing clear urine. A routine antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks documented normal renal tract anatomy, and he is thriving on the 50th centile.

He has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. The ED consultant asks whether imaging is required before discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused; abdomen soft with no mass; genitalia normal circumcised; no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Suprapubic aspirate urine: pure Escherichia coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin; creatinine 32 micromol/L; normal antenatal renal tract ultrasound at 20 weeks

lead_in: What imaging strategy is most appropriate before discharge?

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram planned once the acute illness has resolved
options.rationale: MCUG is not routine in the RCH pathway after a first typical UTI; it is considered only when renal ultrasound is abnormal or infections recur. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to detect renal cortical scarring reliably
options.rationale: DMSA is a NICE construct and is not part of the routine RCH cascade after a first typical UTI in an infant with documented antenatal imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No renal tract imaging is indicated as antenatal ultrasound was normal
options.rationale: For a first typical UTI in an infant under 6 months who responded within 48 hours and had documented normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH does not recommend routine repeat imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks of resolution in the community
options.rationale: RCH reserves post-illness ultrasound for infants without documented antenatal imaging or with atypical UTI; documented normal antenatal scan makes this unnecessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography before discharge from hospital
options.rationale: Contrast voiding urosonography is not part of the standard AU cascade for a first typical UTI and is unnecessary given normal antenatal anatomy and rapid response. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: The RCH UTI cascade in infants distinguishes typical from atypical UTI. Typical UTI (E coli, sensitive to first-line antibiotics, response within 48 hours, no sepsis, no abdominal mass, normal creatinine) requires renal ultrasound only if the child is under 6 months without documented antenatal imaging or if infections recur. Documented normal antenatal anatomy in an infant with a typical UTI removes the ultrasound requirement. DMSA and MCUG are not routine in the RCH pathway; they are NICE constructs.
key_points: Typical UTI in an infant does not always require imaging.
Documented normal antenatal ultrasound removes the routine US indication.
DMSA and MCUG are not in the RCH cascade for typical UTI.
Atypical features trigger US during the acute illness.
explanation.pearls: The RCH pathway asks two questions after a first UTI: was it atypical, and was there documented antenatal imaging; if the answers are no atypical features and yes to antenatal imaging, no follow-up imaging is required.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infections in children

stem:
A 3-month-old former term infant has been on low-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 1 L/min for 90 minutes on the paediatric ward for RSV bronchiolitis. On arrival his SpO2 was 84 percent on room air; it improved to 91 percent on low flow, then dropped to 88 percent over the last 30 minutes. Work of breathing is now increasing with tracheal tug and audible grunting.

He is not feeding, has had a wet nappy 3 hours ago and remains alert. Capillary blood gas at 90 minutes shows pH 7.32, pCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. His mother stayed at the bedside overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 172/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 68/min, SpO2 88 percent on 1 L/min low-flow, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; marked subcostal and intercostal recessions; tracheal tug; audible grunt; wheeze and fine crackles bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR RSV positive; capillary gas pH 7.32, pCO2 52 mmHg (35-45), HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen therapy?

options.text: Continue low-flow oxygen and reassess after another 60 minutes of therapy
options.rationale: The RCH pathway defines low-flow failure at 2 hours as the trigger to escalate; observation with worsening pCO2 and desaturation would delay appropriate escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Increase low-flow oxygen to 3 L/min through the same nasal prong device
options.rationale: Beyond 2 L/min low-flow prong oxygen becomes uncomfortable and inefficient without humidification; the guideline steps to HFNC rather than higher unheated flows. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with a repeat gas in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not recommended in bronchiolitis by RCH; there is no evidence of reduced admission or ventilation and it is a distractor from oxygen escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Escalate to high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 90
options.rationale: RCH escalates from low-flow to HFNC after 2 hours of low-flow failure defined by rising work of breathing, hypoxia or hypercapnia; HFNC 2 L/kg/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent is the next step. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Intubate immediately for mechanical ventilation and transfer to intensive care
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for HFNC failure with impending respiratory failure or apnoea; an alert child with mild hypercapnia should first trial HFNC. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The RCH bronchiolitis pathway escalates oxygen in stepwise fashion: low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min first, HFNC 2 L/kg/min after 2 hours of low-flow failure, and intubation reserved for HFNC failure. Failure is defined by rising respiratory rate, worsening work of breathing, desaturation below the SpO2 90 percent target or hypercapnia. Nebulised adrenaline and salbutamol are not recommended. Escalation timing matters: earlier HFNC does not reduce ICU admission but delaying appropriate step-up when the child is decompensating risks progression to intubation.
key_points: Low-flow first, escalate to HFNC after 2 hours of failure.
HFNC starting dose is 2 L/kg/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent.
Nebulised adrenaline is not recommended in bronchiolitis by RCH.
Intubation is reserved for HFNC failure or apnoea.
explanation.pearls: In bronchiolitis, escalate low-flow to HFNC when 2 hours of low-flow trial has failed on any of rising RR, increased work of breathing, SpO2 below 90 percent, or rising pCO2.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl presented three weeks ago with a palpable purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, right knee arthritis and colicky abdominal pain. Skin biopsy at that admission showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis and she was managed with paracetamol and outpatient follow-up. Symptoms have fully resolved. Blood pressure was normal throughout admission and initial urine dipstick was clear.

She returns for the planned review. Her mother reports she has been well, eating normally and returned to school. The GP has done no interval investigations since discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no residual rash or joint swelling; abdomen soft; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Today: urine dipstick trace protein, no blood; formal urine protein/creatinine ratio pending; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Discharge from follow-up as the acute illness has resolved without complication
options.rationale: HSP nephritis can develop up to 6 months after acute presentation; discharge at 3 weeks misses late-onset nephritis and abandons the standard surveillance window. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Renal biopsy this week to detect and characterise late-onset HSP nephritis
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension or falling GFR; not indicated with trace protein and no other features. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks to prevent renal complications
options.rationale: Steroids do not prevent HSP nephritis onset; they are used only in established significant renal disease or severe extrarenal symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Weekly BP and urine dipstick surveillance for 6 months from initial presentation
options.rationale: RCH recommends weekly BP and urinalysis for the first 2 months then monthly to 6 months; late-onset nephritis is uncommon after 6 months if surveillance is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Immediate nephrology referral for consideration of ACE inhibitor prophylaxis
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are used for established persistent proteinuria; prophylactic use in asymptomatic children with only trace protein at 3 weeks is not recommended. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis is the main long-term complication and can present up to 6 months after the acute illness. Australian surveillance uses weekly blood pressure and urinalysis for the first 2 months, then monthly to 6 months from presentation. Renal referral is triggered by persistent proteinuria, hypertension, macroscopic haematuria, or falling GFR. Steroids do not prevent onset of nephritis and are reserved for established significant renal disease or severe extrarenal symptoms.
key_points: HSP nephritis can develop up to 6 months after acute illness.
Weekly BP and urinalysis for 2 months then monthly to 6 months.
Steroids do not prevent nephritis onset.
Renal referral is triggered by proteinuria, hypertension or falling GFR.
explanation.pearls: After HSP, teach the family to bring the child weekly for BP and urine dipstick for 2 months and monthly to 6 months; refer only when protein persists on formal urine protein to creatinine ratio, BP rises above the 95th centile, or haematuria becomes macroscopic.

stem:
A 14-year-old girl attends the general paediatric clinic with a 12-month history of migraine without aura. She now has 6 attacks per month, each lasting most of a day, and has missed 4 days of school in the last month. Simple analgesics are effective when taken early, and she has responded to oral sumatriptan on 3 occasions. Her diary shows no clear food triggers, sleep is regular, and she is not on any hormonal contraception.

Mother describes similar migraines through her own adolescence. Neurological examination and fundoscopy today are normal, blood pressure is normal for her age and weight is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination and fundoscopy within normal limits; no papilloedema; no meningism; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Headache diary confirms 6 attacks per month over 3 months; MRI brain not indicated on clinical features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic strategy?

options.text: Start oral propranolol 10 mg twice daily and review response at 8 weeks
options.rationale: Propranolol is a first-line paediatric migraine prophylactic per Australian consensus and is favoured over topiramate for adolescent girls because it avoids cognitive side effects and pregnancy-related teratogenicity. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Start oral topiramate 25 mg nightly and titrate slowly to a target 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Topiramate is effective but is teratogenic and causes cognitive side effects; propranolol is preferred first-line in adolescent girls of childbearing potential. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Start oral amitriptyline 10 mg nightly and review response at 8 weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Amitriptyline is second-line paediatric prophylaxis; use follows failure or intolerance of first-line beta blockade or riboflavin trial. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Start rizatriptan 5 mg regularly at bedtime nightly as an oral prophylactic
options.rationale: Triptans are acute abortive agents, not prophylactics; daily use risks medication overuse headache and is not evidence-based prevention. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain with contrast for further diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: MRI is not indicated where examination and history are typical of migraine without red flags; scanning does not change management and delays effective prophylaxis. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Paediatric migraine prophylaxis is offered when headaches occur more than 4 to 6 times per month or cause significant disability. Propranolol is first-line for most adolescents; it is favoured over topiramate in adolescent girls of childbearing potential because topiramate is teratogenic and causes cognitive slowing. Riboflavin, magnesium and coenzyme Q10 have supporting evidence and are often trialled together. Pattern reminder placeholder blocks retained here for parity.
key_points: Prophylaxis is offered for 4 or more disabling attacks per month.
Propranolol is first-line in adolescents including girls of childbearing potential.
Topiramate is teratogenic; avoid as first choice in girls.
Triptans are acute abortives, not preventives.
explanation.pearls: For an adolescent girl with 6 or more migraine days a month, start propranolol 10 mg twice daily and reassess at 8 weeks; reserve topiramate for propranolol failure or asthma coexistence.

subtopic_detail: Positive newborn screen for cystic fibrosis
stem:
A 3-week-old boy is referred urgently by the state newborn screening service. His day 3 immunoreactive trypsinogen was elevated, and second-tier CFTR gene analysis identified two variants: F508del in trans with R117H-7T. He is his parents' first child, weight is on the 50th centile, and he has been feeding well with normal wet nappies and passing stool.

Both parents are white European. The parents are anxious after receiving the phone call the same morning and want to know what will confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused; chest clear; abdomen soft; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: NBS: IRT elevated day 3; CFTR analysis F508del/R117H-7T; family history negative for CF

lead_in: What is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Repeat immunoreactive trypsinogen level at 6 weeks of age in the community
options.rationale: Repeat IRT is not diagnostic; sweat chloride is the confirmatory test once screen and genotype are abnormal. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.text: Sweat chloride test performed once the infant weighs 3 kilograms or more
options.rationale: Sweat chloride by pilocarpine iontophoresis is the diagnostic gold standard; a value 60 mmol/L or above confirms CF, 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate and 29 mmol/L or below excludes CF. Requires at least 3 kg body weight. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.text: Faecal elastase measurement to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
options.rationale: Faecal elastase is used to determine pancreatic sufficiency once CF is diagnosed; it is not a diagnostic test for CF. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.text: Nasal potential difference measurement at the tertiary respiratory service
options.rationale: Nasal PD is reserved for borderline or complex cases after sweat chloride, not first-line diagnostic confirmation. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

options.text: High resolution CT chest to detect early structural bronchiectasis at baseline
options.rationale: HRCT is not part of diagnostic confirmation; screening imaging in early infancy carries radiation and does not establish the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care)
source_refs: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening for CF is a three-tier process: IRT, targeted CFTR mutation panel, then sweat chloride. Sweat testing is diagnostic and required even when two variants are identified because R117H-7T is a variable-consequence mutation whose phenotype cannot be predicted from genotype alone. Sweat chloride requires the infant to weigh at least 3 kg to obtain an adequate sweat volume. A value 60 mmol/L or above is diagnostic; 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate and warrants CF clinic follow-up; 29 mmol/L or below excludes CF.
key_points: Sweat chloride is diagnostic; NBS is screening only.
Cut-offs: 60 or above diagnostic, 30 to 59 intermediate, 29 or below excludes.
Minimum 3 kg body weight for adequate sweat volume.
Faecal elastase determines pancreatic sufficiency after diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: In a screen-positive baby with a variable-consequence CFTR variant like R117H-7T, sweat chloride is mandatory to phenotype the infant; a diagnosis cannot be made or excluded on genotype alone.

sources.label: Australian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care
Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Consensus: Diagnosis of CF

stem:
A 5-year-old boy has 12 months of infrequent bowel motions (once every 4 to 5 days) with increasing daily soiling in his underwear over the last 3 months. He complains of tummy pain that is relieved by passing stool. His mother is embarrassed and stressed because his prep teacher has raised concerns. Diet includes little fruit, adequate fibre otherwise, and he drinks 1 litre of water daily.

He grew normally, has no perianal fissure and no red flags for organic disease. There is no delayed passage of meconium, no family history of Hirschsprung disease. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well; abdomen soft with a palpable indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa; perianal area normal without fissure; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: None; clinical diagnosis of functional constipation with overflow soiling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Behavioural toileting programme alone with review in six weeks in general practice
options.rationale: Behavioural programmes are insufficient when a faecal mass is present; disimpaction must precede maintenance and behavioural work. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Increase dietary fibre and daily fluid intake with a review in four weeks by GP
options.rationale: Diet alone will not clear an established faecal mass; without disimpaction overflow soiling will continue. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Oral macrogol disimpaction protocol titrating dose over 3 to 7 days as tolerated
