options.rationale: RCH first-line disimpaction is oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes, escalated over 3 to 7 days to clear the faecal mass, then transition to maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Rectal phosphate enema now in ED followed by discharge on oral maintenance
options.rationale: Rectal preparations are second-line if oral disimpaction fails; they are more distressing for children and are not the initial step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Manual disimpaction under general anaesthetic in the paediatric surgery day list
options.rationale: Manual disimpaction under GA is a last resort after oral and rectal disimpaction fail; not the initial treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with overflow soiling requires disimpaction before maintenance therapy or behavioural work. Australian first-line disimpaction is oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes, titrated over 3 to 7 days. Maintenance macrogol then continues for at least 6 months and often longer, with a slow wean when regular soft stools are established. Behavioural toileting programmes with rewards, scheduled sits after meals, and dietary support are adjuncts, not substitutes for disimpaction. Rectal enemas and manual disimpaction are reserved for oral disimpaction failure.
key_points: Disimpaction precedes maintenance and behavioural work.
Oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is first-line disimpaction.
Maintenance therapy continues for at least 6 months.
Rectal preparations are second-line if oral fails.
explanation.pearls: In overflow soiling with a palpable faecal mass, start oral macrogol disimpaction titrating up over a week; only if oral fails do you consider a rectal enema.

sources.label: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

stem:
A 20-month-old girl attends general paediatric outpatients with a 3-month history of pallor and reduced energy. She drinks 900 mL of cow's milk a day, eats a limited solid food range and has never accepted red meat. Her weight is on the 25th centile and unchanged from 6 months ago. Blood tests were done in the community 2 weeks ago.

First-line oral iron polymaltose was tried for 2 weeks by her GP; she refused every dose and vomited twice. There is no family history of iron malabsorption, coeliac serology is negative and her mother's antenatal ferritin was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no scleral icterus; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (105-135), MCV 62 fL (75-87), ferritin 6 microgram/L (30-300), CRP 3 mg/L (<5); coeliac serology and faecal occult blood negative; reticulocyte count reduced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Continue oral iron polymaltose 6 mg/kg elemental iron daily for 3 more months
options.rationale: The child has already refused and vomited oral iron; further oral trial is unlikely to succeed and will delay treatment of severe iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Switch to a different oral iron formulation and repeat FBC in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Formulation switching helps mild tolerability issues but does not resolve refusal; with Hb 78 g/L a definitive treatment is needed sooner. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Blood transfusion in day unit with subsequent oral iron maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic instability or symptomatic severe anaemia; iron infusion corrects both the deficit and the anaemia without transfusion risks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion in the paediatric day medical unit
options.rationale: IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) is indicated when oral iron fails or is not tolerated; RCH permits single dose infusion in day unit with monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL daily and review haemoglobin in three months
options.rationale: Milk reduction is essential adjunct but as sole treatment for Hb 78 g/L will not resolve severe deficiency in the required timeframe. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers is commonly driven by high cow's milk intake and inadequate iron in solids. Oral iron 3 to 6 mg/kg elemental daily is first-line, but IV iron is indicated when oral iron is refused, not tolerated or when there is severe anaemia requiring rapid correction. Ferric carboxymaltose is used in Australian paediatric day units with monitoring for hypophosphataemia and infusion reactions. Cow's milk reduction to less than 500 mL per day and dietitian review are essential adjuncts. Blood transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic instability, not for correction of iron stores.
key_points: Oral iron 3 to 6 mg/kg elemental is first-line.
IV iron is indicated for oral failure, refusal or severe deficiency.
Ferric carboxymaltose is standard IV iron in AU paediatrics.
Cow's milk should be limited to under 500 mL per day.
explanation.pearls: When a toddler with Hb under 80 g/L and ferritin under 10 microgram/L refuses oral iron, arrange ferric carboxymaltose day-unit infusion rather than persisting with oral trials.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Blood - Iron deficiency in children

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is admitted from clinic with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and 3 kg unintentional weight loss. Random venous glucose in the surgery was 22 mmol/L. She is alert, warm and well-perfused with normal breathing. Ketones are 1.4 mmol/L on capillary meter and venous blood gas shows pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L. GAD antibodies are pending.

She is otherwise well, on no medications, and eats a mixed carbohydrate diet with 3 main meals and 2 snacks. There is no family history of type 1 diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-hydrated; no Kussmaul breathing; abdomen soft; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Venous glucose 22 mmol/L; capillary ketones 1.4 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L; HbA1c 11.2 percent; U and E within normal limits; weight 34 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial insulin regimen?

options.text: Continuous intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with hourly BSL
options.rationale: IV insulin infusion is used for DKA; this child is not in DKA (pH 7.36, ketones 1.4) so subcutaneous insulin is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: New-onset type 1 diabetes)

options.text: Basal insulin degludec once daily only with no meal-time boluses initially
options.rationale: Basal-only misses postprandial spikes and does not achieve control; a basal-bolus regimen is standard from day 1. (Source: RCH CPG: New-onset type 1 diabetes)

options.text: Twice daily premixed 70/30 insulin with dose split before breakfast and dinner
options.rationale: Premixed BD regimens force meal timing and carbohydrate rigidity; AU paediatric standard is basal-bolus or pump therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: New-onset type 1 diabetes)

options.text: Subcutaneous basal-bolus regimen with glargine and rapid-acting insulin at meals
options.rationale: AU paediatric standard for new-onset T1DM without DKA is a basal-bolus regimen from day 1: long-acting glargine or detemir plus rapid-acting analogue at meals with carbohydrate counting. (Source: RCH CPG: New-onset type 1 diabetes)

options.text: Oral metformin 500 mg twice daily and repeat testing in 6 weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Metformin is not used as initial therapy for type 1 diabetes; insulin is essential from diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: New-onset type 1 diabetes)

explanation.summary: New-onset type 1 diabetes in paediatric practice without DKA is managed with a subcutaneous basal-bolus regimen from day 1. Long-acting insulin (glargine, detemir or degludec) provides basal coverage; rapid-acting analogue at meals covers carbohydrate loads with insulin-to-carbohydrate ratios individualised to the child. Total daily insulin at diagnosis is typically 0.5 to 1 unit/kg/day, split roughly 40 to 50 percent basal and 50 to 60 percent bolus. Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (pump) is an alternative offered by many Australian centres. Metformin is not first-line; insulin is essential.
key_points: Basal-bolus from day 1 is AU paediatric standard.
IV insulin is reserved for DKA (pH under 7.3 or HCO3 under 15).
Total daily insulin at diagnosis 0.5 to 1 unit/kg.
Metformin is not first-line for type 1 diabetes.
explanation.pearls: In new type 1 diabetes without DKA start basal-bolus subcutaneous insulin at 0.5 to 1 unit/kg/day split 40 percent basal and 60 percent rapid-acting at meals; IV insulin is only for DKA.

stem:
A 5-day-old term male infant is transferred from a peripheral hospital because of ongoing hypoglycaemia despite frequent breast feeds and formula top-ups every 3 hours. Birthweight was 4.2 kg and delivery was uncomplicated; mother was screened GDM-negative. The lowest recorded blood glucose has been 1.6 mmol/L, occurring 60 minutes after a feed. Between feeds he is jittery and this settles with feeding.

He is alert, has good tone and no dysmorphic features. There is no birth trauma, cephalohaematoma or midline defect. Free T4 is normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; large for gestational age; no dysmorphism; no midline cleft; genitalia normal; anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 1.6 mmol/L; cortisol, growth hormone, insulin, C-peptide, ammonia, lactate, urine ketones sample sent during hypoglycaemia; free T4 normal for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?

options.text: Send a critical sample for insulin and cortisol at the next hypoglycaemic event
options.rationale: The critical sample taken at the time of hypoglycaemia (glucose under 2.6 mmol/L) is diagnostic; measuring insulin, C-peptide, growth hormone, cortisol, ketones, lactate and ammonia separates hyperinsulinism from counter-regulatory failure and fatty acid oxidation defects. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Empirical intramuscular glucagon 0.5 mg for suspected persistent hyperinsulinism
options.rationale: Glucagon may transiently raise glucose but a positive response does not confirm the cause; diagnosis rests on critical sample results, not empirical therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Immediate MRI head and pituitary before hypoglycaemia is corrected in ED
options.rationale: Panhypopituitarism is one differential; imaging is deferred until biochemistry directs the workup, and MRI is not urgent when treatment can maintain glucose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Trial of diazoxide 5 mg/kg per day orally before formal biochemistry results
options.rationale: Diazoxide is used for confirmed congenital hyperinsulinism after biochemistry supports the diagnosis; empirical use bypasses the diagnostic workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Chromosomal microarray to detect Beckwith-Wiedemann related hyperinsulinism
options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray is directed by phenotype; without dysmorphic features it is not the first investigation, though it may follow. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours needs a critical sample workup because the differential is broad: congenital hyperinsulinism, panhypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency, fatty acid oxidation defects, and inborn errors of gluconeogenesis. The critical sample (glucose, insulin, C-peptide, GH, cortisol, ketones, lactate, ammonia, free fatty acids, acylcarnitine profile) taken at the time of hypoglycaemia allows separation of these causes. Hyperinsulinism is diagnosed when insulin is measurable, ketones and free fatty acids are suppressed, and glycaemic response to glucagon is positive.
key_points: Critical sample must be drawn during hypoglycaemia (BSL under 2.6).
Insulin, C-peptide, GH, cortisol, ketones, FFA, ammonia, lactate all needed.
Suppressed ketones with measurable insulin equals hyperinsulinism.
Diazoxide is confirmation-directed, not empirical.
explanation.pearls: Persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia demands a critical sample at glucose under 2.6 mmol/L; measure insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, ammonia and lactate together before any therapeutic trial.

stem:
A 6-year-old girl weighing 22 kg had biphasic anaphylaxis 4 hours ago after accidental cashew ingestion at a birthday party. She received 300 microgram intramuscular adrenaline at the first symptom onset with rapid resolution, and a second 300 microgram dose 3 hours later when hoarseness, wheeze and hypotension recurred. She has again responded fully and vital signs are normal.

She has a documented cashew allergy and carries her own EpiPen. She has no asthma and no previous ICU admissions. Both parents are present, competent and speak English fluently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no rash currently; chest clear with no wheeze; oropharynx normal; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: No acute investigations required beyond clinical monitoring; ECG unremarkable

lead_in: What is the minimum appropriate observation period from the second adrenaline dose?

options.text: Two hours of observation because response to the second dose has been complete
options.rationale: Two hours is insufficient after biphasic reaction; ASCIA recommends longer observation with any biphasic feature or second adrenaline dose. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Four hours after the second adrenaline dose provided the child remains stable
options.rationale: Four hours applies to a straightforward single-dose responder; biphasic reactions require extended observation. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Twelve hours of hospital observation because of biphasic pattern and second dose
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends at least 12 hours observation after biphasic reactions or after a second adrenaline dose; discharge earlier misses further recurrence in the higher risk window. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Twenty-four hours of admission and paediatric high dependency unit review
options.rationale: HDU is reserved for haemodynamically unstable or ventilated patients; a stable child does not require 24-hour HDU stay. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Forty-eight hours of admission because of confirmed food-triggered anaphylaxis
options.rationale: 48-hour admission is not standard; extended observation is guided by clinical features not by trigger type alone. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ASCIA recommends a minimum 4-hour observation after uncomplicated single-dose anaphylaxis, and at least 12 hours after any biphasic reaction, any second adrenaline dose or ongoing bronchospasm. Biphasic reactions occur in around 5 percent of anaphylaxis presentations and typically re-emerge within 12 hours. Discharge planning must include a personal ASCIA Action Plan, replacement adrenaline autoinjectors on hand, allergy specialist referral, and demonstrated correct use of the device by the family.
key_points: Single-dose responder: 4 hours minimum observation.
Biphasic reaction or second dose: 12 hours minimum observation.
Discharge requires ASCIA Action Plan and autoinjector on hand.
HDU only if haemodynamically unstable or ventilated.
explanation.pearls: After a biphasic anaphylaxis or when 2 adrenaline doses have been required, observe for at least 12 hours regardless of how well the child appears at hour 4.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics for meningitis in a young infant
stem:
A 6-week-old former term boy is brought to a regional ED with 12 hours of fever, poor feeding and increasing irritability. He is difficult to console, has a full anterior fontanelle and mottled peripheries. Capillary refill centrally is 3 seconds. Bloods and lumbar puncture have been obtained without difficulty and blood culture is drawn.

He is exclusively breastfed, has had all birth screening, and has no known immunodeficiency. His parents are Australian and there is no unusual travel or contact history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but inconsolable; full anterior fontanelle; mottled peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; no rash
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 480/mm3 (85 percent neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 1.6 mmol/L with plasma 5.4 mmol/L; Gram stain negative; blood culture drawn; WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily as sole empirical antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin and is avoided in neonates and young infants where kernicterus risk remains; cefotaxime is preferred and Listeria cover is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours and gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: The neonatal sepsis penicillin-gentamicin combination is used up to 4 weeks; at 6 weeks the CSF-active third generation cephalosporin plus amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours as monotherapy for CSF cover
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added when pneumococcal disease is suspected and resistance is a concern; monotherapy misses Listeria and gram-negatives. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 hours and amoxicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours
options.rationale: This combination is correct in principle but dexamethasone should be considered concurrently for infants with pneumococcal or Hib meningitis suspicion; the fully correct answer includes dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg 6-hourly, amoxicillin 50 mg/kg 6-hourly plus dexamethasone
options.rationale: In infants under 3 months, empirical therapy is cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover); dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly for 4 days is given with or just before the first antibiotic if bacterial meningitis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Empirical antibiotic therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in an infant aged over 4 weeks and under 3 months is intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin to cover common pathogens (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes). Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus risk. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days is recommended when Haemophilus influenzae type b or pneumococcal meningitis is suspected, ideally given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae.
key_points: Cefotaxime plus amoxicillin covers common pathogens under 3 months.
Ceftriaxone avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement.
Amoxicillin covers Listeria in under 3 months.
Dexamethasone with or before first antibiotic when bacterial meningitis suspected.
explanation.pearls: In a young infant with suspected meningitis, start cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus dexamethasone concurrently; do not use ceftriaxone under 3 months and do not delay dexamethasone until organism is known.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia was in the same primary school classroom as another child who developed a chickenpox rash yesterday. His medical team confirms he received VZV vaccination pre-diagnosis but has not had chickenpox. He has been on maintenance chemotherapy for 8 months and his most recent lymphocyte count was 0.6 x10^9/L. Contact occurred 20 hours ago in an indoor setting for over an hour.

He is currently well with no fever, malaise or rash. His mother contacted the oncology fellow this morning to ask what to do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 100/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well; no rash; oropharynx clear; abdomen soft; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0); recent varicella IgG antibody titre pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure management?

options.text: Zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) intramuscular within 96 hours of contact today
options.rationale: ZIG is indicated for significant exposure in a susceptible immunocompromised child and is most effective within 96 hours (up to 10 days); on maintenance chemotherapy, prior vaccination cannot be assumed to confer protection. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Give the varicella live-attenuated vaccine within 5 days of the contact today
options.rationale: Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy because of dissemination risk; ZIG is the passive prophylaxis choice. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg 4 times daily for 7 days immediately as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aciclovir may be used from day 7 to 14 post-exposure as an alternative when ZIG is unavailable; ZIG is first-line if within window. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: No action; the vaccine received before diagnosis provides adequate ongoing protection
options.rationale: Chemotherapy suppresses vaccine-induced immunity; a pre-diagnosis vaccine cannot be assumed protective and passive prophylaxis is required. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Admit today for intravenous immunoglobulin and prolonged inpatient monitoring
options.rationale: IVIG is not the equivalent product for VZV post-exposure prophylaxis; specific ZIG is used and can be given as an outpatient. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

explanation.summary: Post-exposure varicella prophylaxis in an immunocompromised child uses zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) intramuscularly, ideally within 96 hours of significant contact and up to 10 days. Significant contact is defined as face-to-face contact of 5 minutes or more, or over 1 hour in the same indoor space. Prior varicella vaccination cannot be assumed protective during chemotherapy because immunosuppression suppresses vaccine responses. Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy. Oral aciclovir from day 7 to 14 post-exposure is an alternative if ZIG is unavailable.
key_points: ZIG within 96 hours (up to 10 days) for immunocompromised contacts.
Significant contact: 5 min face-to-face or 1 hour indoors.
Live vaccines contraindicated during chemotherapy.
Aciclovir day 7 to 14 is second-line if ZIG unavailable.
explanation.pearls: For an immunocompromised child exposed to varicella, arrange ZIG within 96 hours; do not rely on pre-chemotherapy vaccine history and do not use live vaccine.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Chickenpox exposure in an immunocompromised child

stem:
A 4-month-old boy presents to the paediatric emergency department with 3 days of coryza, cough and increasing work of breathing. He is bottle-feeding at about 50 percent of normal intake and has had wet nappies overnight. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with no neonatal issues and is fully immunised for age.

On arrival he has audible wheeze with mild subcostal recession. He accepts a small feed on your assessment and settles when held. His SpO2 on room air is 89 percent and stays at 89 to 90 percent when he is calm and awake.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure not routinely measured, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 89 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink centrally; mild subcostal recession; widespread expiratory wheeze and fine crackles; capillary refill under 2 seconds; anterior fontanelle flat
data_table.Investigations: No routine bloods or chest X-ray required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen strategy?

options.text: Give low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min targeting SpO2 at or above 90 percent
options.rationale: RCH CPG uses low-flow nasal prong oxygen as first-line when SpO2 drops below 90 percent when awake, with 90 percent as the maintenance target. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Withhold oxygen and observe overnight because he remains alert and feeding
options.rationale: Sustained awake SpO2 below 90 percent meets the RCH threshold for oxygen therapy irrespective of feeding. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg once before considering any oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for infants under 12 months with typical bronchiolitis in the RCH pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start CPAP via a paediatric interface at 6 cm H2O and admit to ICU immediately
options.rationale: CPAP or intubation follows escalation through low-flow then HFNC when respiratory failure develops; it is not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min heated humidified oxygen now
options.rationale: HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after a trial of at least 1 to 2 hours; it is not the first oxygen escalation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses SpO2 of 90 percent as the maintenance target for infants over 6 weeks with typical bronchiolitis, and starts oxygen with low-flow nasal prongs at 1 to 2 L/min when SpO2 falls below 90 percent awake. HFNC is reserved for infants who fail low-flow after a 1 to 2 hour trial. Bronchodilators, steroids, adrenaline and antibiotics are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis. The pathway is one of supportive feeding, oxygenation and minimal handling.
key_points: SpO2 target on the RCH pathway is 90 percent, not 92 to 94 percent.
Low-flow nasal prongs 1 to 2 L/min are first-line oxygen.
HFNC follows failure of low-flow after 1 to 2 hours.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: On the RCH CPG start nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min once SpO2 sits below 90 percent when the infant is calm and awake; only escalate to HFNC after 1 to 2 hours of failed low-flow.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department at midnight with a barking cough and hoarse voice for 6 hours. She has a mild coryzal illness for 2 days. She is fully immunised, was born at term with no neonatal issues and has never previously been hospitalised.

On arrival she is alert, sitting comfortably in her father's arms and has an audible barking cough with intermittent inspiratory stridor when upset. Between episodes of crying she has no stridor at rest and mild suprasternal recession only when distressed. She accepts a sip of water.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure not measured, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, barking cough on examination; stridor with crying only; no drooling; chest clear to auscultation between coughs
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first steroid dose?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once now and reassess after 2 hours
options.rationale: Prednisolone is second-line to dexamethasone in Australian croup pathways because of shorter duration and reduced evidence base. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once now and observe for at least 30 minutes
options.rationale: RCH CPG dexamethasone dose for mild to moderate croup is 0.15 mg/kg orally; observation continues until stridor at rest resolves. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once now and admit for overnight monitoring
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and respiratory distress; this presentation is mild to moderate. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once and discharge home after 15 minutes of observation
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is an alternative when oral is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is first-line and observation is longer. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with no steroid until stridor at rest returns
options.rationale: Adrenaline is added for severe croup or stridor at rest; steroids are still given at the same time to reduce rebound. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: The RCH croup pathway uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as the default dose for mild to moderate croup. Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked respiratory distress warrants 0.6 mg/kg oral dexamethasone plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 as a flat dose (not weight-based). After nebulised adrenaline the child must be observed for at least 3 hours from the last dose because of rebound. Prednisolone is second-line if dexamethasone is unavailable. Nebulised budesonide 2 mg is an alternative when oral steroid is not tolerated.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally is standard for mild to moderate croup on the RCH pathway.
0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 and requires 3 hours observation.
Steroids are given alongside adrenaline to reduce rebound.
explanation.pearls: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup and reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup with resting stridor. Adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 and mandates 3 hours of observation from the last dose.

stem:
A 22-month-old boy presents with 24 hours of watery non-bloody diarrhoea (six loose stools today) and three episodes of non-bilious vomiting. He weighs 12 kg. His mother reports reduced but not absent oral intake and one wet nappy in the past 8 hours. There has been no fever, no rash and no unwell contacts other than a similar mild illness in his older sibling.

On arrival he is clingy but consolable, has slightly dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor over the abdomen. Capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally, extremities are warm. He gags on the first oral rehydration sip and vomits it back within 5 minutes despite a small volume.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mildly dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 seconds central; abdomen soft, non-tender; no rash; weight 12 kg (usual 12.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: No routine bloods indicated at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Admit for IV maintenance fluids alone without any enteral rehydration attempt
options.rationale: Maintenance IV fluid does not replace the existing deficit; enteral rehydration is preferred where feasible. (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert an IV cannula and give 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 20 minutes now
options.rationale: IV rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or failure of enteral rehydration; a nasogastric trial is preferred first. (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and give oral rehydration solution at 20 mL/kg over 1 hour
options.rationale: RCH CPG recommends nasogastric rehydration as first-line when oral intake fails in mild to moderate dehydration; NG delivery avoids gag-triggered vomiting. (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Discharge home with advice to offer small frequent oral fluids and review in 4 hours
options.rationale: He has failed one oral trial in your presence and shows features of mild to moderate dehydration; discharge without a rehydration trial is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give a single oral ondansetron 4 mg and repeat oral rehydration attempt after 20 minutes
options.rationale: Ondansetron 2 mg is the dose for 8 to 15 kg children in RCH and 4 mg is the 15 to 30 kg dose; nasogastric rehydration is the preferred escalation. (Source: RCH CPG Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: RCH CPG for paediatric gastroenteritis places nasogastric rehydration as first-line when oral rehydration fails in mild to moderate dehydration, with IV rehydration reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or failure of the NG trial. Oral rehydration solution delivered by NG is generally 20 mL/kg over 1 hour repeated as needed. Ondansetron single-dose supports oral rehydration in vomiting children at weight-banded doses: 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg and 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg. Antibiotics are reserved for specific proven pathogens.
key_points: Nasogastric rehydration is first-line in mild to moderate dehydration failing oral trials.
IV bolus 20 mL/kg is for severe dehydration, shock or NG failure.
Ondansetron oral dose is banded: 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg.
Discharge without a rehydration trial is unsafe with dry mucous membranes and reduced turgor.
explanation.pearls: In a 12 kg child with mild to moderate dehydration who cannot keep oral fluids down, RCH recommends nasogastric ORS at 20 mL/kg over 1 hour before any IV cannulation.

stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with a rectal temperature of 38.4 degrees C recorded at home and confirmed on arrival. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with an uneventful pregnancy and postnatal course. He has been feeding poorly for 12 hours and has had reduced wet nappies today, with two brief episodes of pallor described by his mother.

On examination he is alert but has a weak cry and is difficult to rouse for feeds. His anterior fontanelle is flat, capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally, and the abdomen is soft. There is no rash, no bulging fontanelle and no localising focus. He has not received any recent vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 74/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weak cry; capillary refill 3 seconds central; anterior fontanelle flat; chest clear; abdomen soft; no rash; no focal source
data_table.Investigations: Point of care glucose 4.2 mmol/L (2.6-6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next set of investigations and treatment?

options.text: Blood tests and urine dipstick only and start oral amoxicillin after clean-catch urine
options.rationale: Oral therapy and dipstick-only sampling are inadequate for a sick febrile infant under 3 months; parenteral empirical antibiotics are needed. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile child)

options.text: Observation for 6 hours with paracetamol and only investigate if temperature rises further
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is unsafe in an unwell-appearing infant under 3 months with fever; empirical antibiotics must not be delayed. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile child)

options.text: Chest X-ray, viral swab, blood cultures and inhaled bronchodilator without lumbar puncture
options.rationale: The presentation is not respiratory-focused and LP is mandatory in an unwell infant under 3 months with fever unless immediately contraindicated. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile child)

options.text: Full septic workup including lumbar puncture followed by IV cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin now
options.rationale: Any unwell-appearing infant under 3 months with fever needs a full septic workup including LP and empirical IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin per RCH sepsis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile child)

options.text: Blood cultures, urine microscopy and IV ceftriaxone with observation only for 4 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not preferred in the first weeks due to bilirubin displacement; LP cannot be deferred in an unwell-appearing infant under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG Febrile child)

explanation.summary: RCH guidance for the febrile infant under 3 months mandates a full septic workup including blood culture, urine microscopy and culture, chest X-ray if respiratory symptoms are present, and lumbar puncture in any unwell-appearing infant or under 28 days old. Empirical parenteral antibiotics are IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) to cover Listeria in the first weeks of life; ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement. Delay in antibiotics is a major cause of preventable death. Well-appearing infants aged 1 to 3 months follow a stepwise pathway but still receive full culture set and empirical antibiotics if criteria are unmet.
key_points: Unwell infants under 3 months need full septic workup including LP.
Empirical antibiotics are cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin in the first weeks.
Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates due to bilirubin displacement.
Delay in antibiotics is a preventable cause of paediatric sepsis death.
explanation.pearls: For a 5 week old with fever and any red flag (weak cry, poor feeding, cap refill above 2 seconds) do the full septic workup with LP and give IV cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin without waiting for cultures.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents with 12 hours of fever, lethargy and a non-blanching rash on her legs that has spread to her trunk over the past hour. She has been unwell since yesterday with 24 hours of vomiting and reduced oral intake. She is fully immunised and previously well. Her weight is 15 kg.

On arrival she is drowsy but rouseable, has cool peripheries, capillary refill of 4 seconds centrally and a non-blanching purpuric rash on her lower limbs and abdomen. Her SpO2 is 96 percent on room air and she has no stridor, wheeze or focal chest signs. Point of care lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rouseable; capillary refill 4 seconds central; cool peripheries; non-blanching rash on lower limbs and abdomen; no meningism yet
data_table.Investigations: Point of care lactate 4.2 mmol/L; venous access not yet obtained

lead_in: What is the correct order for the first three resuscitation actions?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, then take blood cultures, then give antibiotics
options.rationale: Blood cultures must be drawn before antibiotics ideally but antibiotic delivery must not be delayed by fluid; culture then antibiotic is preferred once access is secured. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Start adrenaline infusion first, then obtain access and then give antibiotics after fluids
options.rationale: Inotropes are added only after 40 to 60 mL/kg fluid fails to restore perfusion; they are not the opening move. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture immediately for CSF then give antibiotics tailored to CSF findings
options.rationale: LP is deferred until circulation is stable and coagulation is safe; empirical antibiotics must not wait for CSF in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Intubate first for airway protection then obtain access and give antibiotics after airway is secured
options.rationale: Intubation is not the first step in an alert though drowsy 3 year old with adequate SpO2; resuscitation and antibiotics come first. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Obtain IV or intraosseous access, take blood cultures, then give first IV antibiotic within the hour
options.rationale: The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway is IV/IO access, blood cultures, then first antibiotic within the sepsis-6 hour, before fluid bolus is delivered. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

explanation.summary: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences resuscitation as: obtain IV or intraosseous access within minutes, draw blood cultures (do not delay antibiotics for this), give the first IV antibiotic within the hour, and start 20 mL/kg saline boluses (over 5 to 10 minutes) repeated to a total of 40 to 60 mL/kg while reassessing. Inotropes such as adrenaline are started when perfusion remains poor after fluid resuscitation. Lumbar puncture is deferred in septic shock until the child is stable and coagulation is safe.
key_points: Sequence is access, cultures, first antibiotic within the hour.
Fluid boluses are 20 mL/kg saline over 5 to 10 minutes to a total of 40 to 60 mL/kg.
Inotropes come after fluid fails, not before.
LP is deferred in shock until circulation is stable.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric septic shock the hour bundle is IO/IV access, blood cultures, empirical antibiotics and 20 mL/kg saline boluses to 60 mL/kg; adrenaline starts if perfusion stays poor after fluids.

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging pathway in a toddler
stem:
A 20-month-old girl is brought to your general practice for review one week after her first confirmed urinary tract infection. She had 48 hours of fever and irritability, urine culture grew Escherichia coli with clean-catch collection, and she was treated with 5 days of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She defervesced within 36 hours of starting antibiotics.

She is now clinically well with normal feeding and activity. She had an unremarkable antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks that documented normal kidneys and bladder. She has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, no palpable abdominal mass on examination today, and no growth concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure not routinely measured, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and active; abdomen soft with no palpable mass; genitalia normal; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture from admission grew E coli fully sensitive; renal function during illness within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No routine imaging required now; safety-net for recurrence and any atypical features later
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a well child under 24 months with a normal antenatal scan. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram within 4 weeks to identify any vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive with radiation exposure and is not indicated after a typical single UTI in the RCH cascade. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Start daily prophylactic trimethoprim for 6 months and re-image only if breakthrough occurs
options.rationale: Long-term prophylaxis is not indicated after a single typical UTI in a well child. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks and a follow-up ultrasound at 12 months routinely
options.rationale: Routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI is not on the RCH pathway when antenatal imaging was normal. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA scan at 6 months regardless of ultrasound findings
options.rationale: RCH does not routinely require DMSA after a first typical UTI in a well child; DMSA is a NICE construct. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

explanation.summary: RCH guidance for a first UTI in a well child under 24 months with normal antenatal imaging does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, DMSA or MCUG. Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical UTI - poor response to 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, non-E coli organism, sepsis, abdominal mass or raised creatinine. Infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring get ultrasound after a first UTI. DMSA and MCUG are not part of the standard RCH cascade; they are NICE constructs. The family should be safety-netted for recurrence.
key_points: First typical UTI in a well child over 6 months does not need routine ultrasound if antenatal scan was normal.
Ultrasound during illness is only for atypical UTI.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH cascade.
Recurrent UTIs prompt further imaging and referral.
explanation.pearls: Do not order routine renal ultrasound after a single typical UTI in a well toddler with a normal antenatal renal scan; safety-net for recurrence and reserve imaging for atypical features.

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis IM adrenaline in a marginal-weight child
stem:
A 5-year-old girl with a known peanut allergy is brought to your remote clinic 15 minutes after biting into a satay skewer at a family barbecue. She has developed a widespread urticarial rash, hoarse voice, one episode of vomiting and audible wheeze. Her mother reports she weighs approximately 19 kg (recent GP weight was 18.6 kg). She has no other medical history and takes no regular medications.

On arrival she is anxious with visible tongue swelling and audible bilateral wheeze. She has a soft stridor at rest and is starting to look pale. Your clinic stocks the current PBS anaphylaxis kits: EpiPen Jr 150 microgram autoinjector and EpiPen 300 microgram autoinjector, plus 1 mg/mL adrenaline ampoules and 1 mL syringes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 82/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tongue swelling, urticarial rash, wheeze bilaterally, stridor at rest, pale peripheries; alert but anxious
data_table.Investigations: Weight documented as 18.6 kg 4 weeks ago; mother estimates 19 kg today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first adrenaline dose to give right now?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 microgram intravenous bolus after establishing IV access first
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is a specialist manoeuvre reserved for refractory anaphylaxis; IM is first-line and must not be delayed for IV access. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscular via EpiPen Jr autoinjector into the mid outer thigh
options.rationale: ASCIA uses a banded age and weight table; children 10 to 20 kg get 150 microgram IM as EpiPen Jr, regardless of exact per kg calculation. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 190 microgram intramuscular calculated as 10 microgram per kg from the ampoule
options.rationale: ASCIA uses banded dosing and specifically avoids weight-based arithmetic in acute anaphylaxis where autoinjectors are available; 10 microgram per kg is not the AU standard. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 300 microgram intramuscular via EpiPen autoinjector into the mid outer thigh
options.rationale: The 300 microgram EpiPen band starts at 20 kg per ASCIA; at 18.6 to 19 kg she falls in the 10 to 20 kg band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Adrenaline 500 microgram intramuscular drawn from a 1 mg per mL ampoule now
options.rationale: 500 microgram is an adult dose over 12 years or above 50 kg per ASCIA; not appropriate for a 19 kg child. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded age and weight table for IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis to avoid dosing errors in a time-critical resuscitation. The bands are 7.5 to 10 kg = 100 microgram (0.1 mL of 1:1000 by ampoule; EpiPen Jr not preferred at this weight), 10 to 20 kg = 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr), 20 to 50 kg = 300 microgram (EpiPen), and above 50 kg or 12 years and older = 500 microgram (EpiPen ampoule-drawn or two EpiPens). Repeat every 5 minutes as needed. Time to IM adrenaline is the leading determinant of survival and must not be delayed for IV access, antihistamines or steroids.
key_points: ASCIA bands: 10 to 20 kg gets 150 microgram IM.
20 to 50 kg gets 300 microgram; above 50 kg or 12+ years gets 500 microgram.
Avoid 10 microgram per kg arithmetic in acute anaphylaxis.
IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases.
explanation.pearls: For a 19 kg child in anaphylaxis give EpiPen Jr 150 microgram IM into the mid outer thigh immediately; do not do mg per kg maths and do not wait for IV access.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid strategy with cerebral oedema risk factors
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents to your tertiary paediatric emergency after 24 hours of Kussmaul breathing, vomiting and progressive drowsiness. She weighs 28 kg. She was well until 3 weeks ago when polyuria and 4 kg weight loss began. On arrival she is drowsy but obeys commands intermittently (GCS 13), has deep sighing respiration and warm dry skin. Her mother reports she has become more confused in the last hour of transport.

Her arterial blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, corrected sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, and ketones 6.2 mmol/L. She has not yet received IV fluids or insulin. Her intravenous cannula is in situ and blood cultures are drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min deep, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; Kussmaul breathing; warm dry skin; capillary refill 3 seconds central; no focal neurology; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: pH 6.98; HCO3 4 mmol/L (22-32); glucose 34 mmol/L (3.5-7.7); Na 128 mmol/L (135-145) corrected 133; K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); ketones 6.2 mmol/L; weight 28 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Withhold all IV fluid until insulin infusion has run for 1 hour to observe glucose trend first with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: DKA is a fluid-deficit state; withholding fluid is unsafe and delays circulatory correction. (Source: RCH CPG Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours titrated to point-of-care glucose without any IV insulin as the sole intervention
options.rationale: SC insulin is used for mild DKA without severe acidosis; severe DKA at pH 6.98 needs a titratable IV insulin infusion. (Source: RCH CPG Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 10 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 30 minutes then start maintenance plus replacement calculated over 48 hours; insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour
options.rationale: ISPAD and RCH DKA guidance in severe DKA with cerebral oedema risk uses a conservative 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes, deficit replacement over 48 hours, and delayed insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour to minimise osmotic shifts. (Source: RCH CPG Diabetic ketoacidosis; ISPAD Consensus Guidelines)

options.text: 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 20 minutes twice then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Rapid fluid loading and immediate high-rate insulin raise the risk of cerebral oedema in a child with drowsiness, new diagnosis and severe acidosis. (Source: RCH CPG Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the pH before any insulin is given with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in paediatric DKA increases cerebral oedema risk and worsens intracellular acidosis; it is not routinely given. (Source: RCH CPG Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: In severe paediatric DKA with cerebral oedema risk factors (age under 5, new diagnosis, severe acidosis with pH under 7.1, drowsiness on arrival, high urea, low pCO2, corrected sodium not rising with therapy), RCH and ISPAD advise a conservative 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 minutes rather than 20 mL/kg, calculating fluid deficit as 5 to 10 percent of body weight and replacing over 48 hours (not 24). Insulin infusion is started at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after the first hour and not before, to minimise osmotic shifts. Bicarbonate is avoided. Potassium is added to fluids once serum K is less than 5.5 and urine output is confirmed.
key_points: Cerebral oedema risk factors call for 10 mL/kg (not 20) bolus over 30 minutes.
Deficit is replaced over 48 hours in severe DKA.
Insulin starts at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after the first hour.
Bicarbonate is avoided in paediatric DKA.
explanation.pearls: In a drowsy 9 year old with new type 1 DM and pH 6.98, use a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, 48 hour deficit replacement and 0.05 unit/kg/hour insulin started after 1 hour; do not use 20 mL/kg boluses or bicarbonate.

stem:
A 4-month-old boy presents to your emergency department with two days of coryza followed by increased work of breathing overnight. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, is exclusively breastfed and has taken about half his usual feeds today. He has had no fever above 38 degrees C at home. There is no family history of asthma.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms with visible subcostal recession, occasional expiratory wheeze and widespread fine crackles bilaterally. Capillary refill is under two seconds. A nasopharyngeal viral swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Nursing staff have placed him on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute, with SpO2 now stable at 91 percent, and he has managed a further breastfeed since arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 90/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 58/min, SpO2 91 percent on 1 L/min nasal prong, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, subcostal recession, mild tracheal tug, widespread expiratory wheeze and fine crackles
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; capillary blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 46 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing respiratory support plan?

options.text: Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen, re-assess in two hours, and only escalate to high-flow nasal cannula if this fails
options.rationale: RCH guidance is low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min targeting SpO2 90 percent or above, with HFNC reserved for failure of low-flow after around two hours of observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Switch immediately to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min because low-flow oxygen is inadequate in RSV bronchiolitis
options.rationale: HFNC is not first-line and is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after a period of trial; leaping straight to HFNC is not RCH-consistent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Aim for SpO2 above 94 percent by titrating oxygen upward on the current nasal prong device
options.rationale: The RCH target for bronchiolitis is SpO2 at or above 90 percent, not above 94 percent; higher targets prolong admission without outcome benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg alongside oxygen while planning any escalation of respiratory support
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no established benefit in typical infant bronchiolitis and is not recommended by RCH; oxygen support alone is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Cease supplemental oxygen and observe on room air since the current SpO2 is above the accepted target
options.rationale: Ceasing oxygen when SpO2 is only just at 91 percent risks desaturation with feeds and sleep; continued low-flow with reassessment is safer. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in an otherwise well infant is supportive care: minimal handling, oxygen for hypoxia, and small frequent or NGT feeds if sucking is impaired. The RCH pathway starts with low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min for SpO2 below 90 percent, targeting 90 percent or above. HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow after approximately two hours, and CPAP or intubation for HFNC failure or apnoea. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, adrenaline nebulisers, chest physiotherapy and antibiotics are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis.
key_points: First-line respiratory support is low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min.
SpO2 target is 90 percent or above; higher targets prolong admission.
HFNC is reserved for low-flow failure after around two hours.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not first-line in typical bronchiolitis.
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis pathway: low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min with SpO2 target 90 percent; only escalate to HFNC after around two hours of failed low-flow.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to your regional emergency department by her father at 2 am with a barky cough and hoarse voice for six hours. She had a runny nose the day before but no fever above 38 degrees C, no drooling and no history of choking. She has had no previous episodes and is fully immunised. Her weight today is 12 kg.

On assessment she is alert, sitting in her father's lap and interacting. She has audible stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession at rest and no cyanosis. Air entry is equal bilaterally with no wheeze. She has taken sips of water without difficulty. There is no obvious lymphadenopathy. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Barky cough, hoarse voice, stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession, no drooling, no accessory muscle use at rest
data_table.Investigations: Not required for typical croup

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dosing plan now?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 solution alone and observe for a further four hours without oral steroid
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for severe or worsening croup; a single steroid dose is the mainstay of treatment even for mild and moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kilogram as a single dose with discharge planning after observation
options.rationale: RCH uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram as a single dose with admission for at least six hours of observation
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the RCH dose reserved for severe croup; using it for moderate croup adds no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram once daily for three days as an equivalent alternative to dexamethasone
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is preferred over multi-day prednisolone in RCH pathways for croup because a single dose covers the illness course. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kilogram given together for additive airway effect
options.rationale: Budesonide adds no clinically important benefit over oral dexamethasone alone and is not first-line at RCH. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis producing subglottic oedema. Severity is graded by stridor at rest, chest wall recession, oxygen saturation and mental state. Corticosteroid is given to all children with croup, including mild, because it shortens symptoms and reduces re-presentation. The RCH dose is 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone for mild or moderate croup, 0.6 mg/kg for severe. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, using a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 (not per-kg), and requires at least three hours of observation after the last dose because of rebound.
key_points: All croup severities receive a single dose of oral dexamethasone.
0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate; 0.6 mg/kg reserved for severe.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000 for severe croup.
Observation is at least three hours after last nebulised adrenaline.
explanation.pearls: RCH uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup and 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup; nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1 in 1000.

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months full septic workup
stem:
A 6-week-old term boy is brought to your metropolitan emergency department by his parents after a measured axillary temperature of 38.4 degrees C at home. He is exclusively breastfed. Over the last twelve hours he has become sleepier than usual with feeds shorter than his previous pattern and one episode of non-bilious vomiting after a feed. There has been no diarrhoea and his wet nappy count is reduced from ten to six today.

On arrival he is pale but rousable, with mild tachycardia and cool peripheries. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no rash and no focal source on examination. Capillary refill centrally is three seconds. Weight is on the 25th percentile and has fallen from the 50th on the growth chart since his six-week check. He has never had a septic workup.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, sleepy but rousable, cool peripheries, soft fontanelle, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care venous glucose 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); capillary lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urine dipstick pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management pathway?

options.text: Send a bagged urine specimen and observe on the ward for six hours before deciding about further investigations
options.rationale: Bagged urine has unacceptable contamination rates in an unwell febrile infant under three months; a sterile catheter or suprapubic sample is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take blood cultures, start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, and defer the lumbar puncture until the child is more stable
options.rationale: Any unwell infant under three months warrants full septic workup including LP before or shortly after antibiotics if safe; deferring the LP indefinitely is inappropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Perform full septic workup including catheter urine, blood cultures and lumbar puncture, then give empirical intravenous cefotaxime
options.rationale: For any unwell infant under three months with fever, RCH mandates full septic workup and empirical intravenous cefotaxime after cultures are drawn. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral paracetamol 15 mg per kilogram and reassess response over the next hour before further tests
options.rationale: Antipyretic response does not exclude serious bacterial infection and should not delay a full septic workup in an unwell infant under three months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Request a same-day outpatient viral polymerase chain reaction panel and discharge home with a red flag advice sheet
options.rationale: Discharge without workup is unsafe in an infant under three months with fever plus reduced feeding and prolonged capillary refill. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Fever in an infant under three months warrants a low threshold for serious bacterial infection because signs are non-specific and meningitis and urinary tract infection are common causes. The RCH pathway is full septic workup - blood, urine (catheter or SPA), and CSF where safe - followed by empirical intravenous cefotaxime. Infants under 28 days always receive septic workup regardless of appearance. Infants 28 days to three months who appear unwell or have abnormal observations follow the same pathway; well-appearing infants in that age band still have blood and urine cultures at a minimum.
key_points: Any unwell infant under three months with fever needs full septic workup.
LP is included where safe; do not defer indefinitely for stability.
Empirical antibiotic is intravenous cefotaxime after cultures.
Bagged urine is not acceptable in this age group.
explanation.pearls: In unwell infants under three months with fever, take blood, catheter urine and CSF then start intravenous cefotaxime; do not rely on antipyretic response to reassure.
